content: Lean 4.15 (from late 2024) shipped Kyle Miller's lean4#6189. The PR description sounds dry and technical, and to my knowledge it went under everyone's radar (edit: not entirely, see the discussion below), but the feature is actually a big deal. I have written a blog post that introduces the feature and argues why we should be using it much more: https://juliahimmel.de/blog/an-underappreciated-lean-feature/
Wow! Very useful feature. I didn't know about this at all. Thanks for letting me know!

This is indeed a feature I discovered really recently, thanks to Mathlib in fact ! A few months ago I was surprised to see a bunch of lemmas under the Submodule.IsCompl namespace (many of these are now deprecated, but for an unrelated reason) : I assumed dot notation would then not work, and whoever wrote them actually forgot to go out of the namespace. But then @Monica Omar (IIRC) made me realize that in fact as long as you open Submodule (which almost every relevant file does), this lets you use dot notation as usual.

That said, I am sometimes (very mildly) concerned by the fact that namespacing has such a wide semantincs in Lean: when you read a name with a bunch of namespaces, it's sometimes hard to know which part is about dot notation and which is about putting things in their logical places.

For example, in docs#Submodule.IsCompl.isTopCompl_of_isClosed, the Submodule and the IsCompl part have distinct roles, while in docs#Submodule.IsTopCompl.continuous_projectionOnto the whole Submodule.IsTopCompl is here for dot notation.

Anatole Dedecker said:

That said, I am sometimes (very mildly) concerned by the fact that namespacing has such a wide semantincs in Lean: when you read a name with a bunch of namespaces, it's sometimes hard to know which part is about dot notation and which is about putting things in their logical places.

This is also bothering me. There appear to be several different (and conflicting!) organizational principles currently in use in Mathlib. Functionality that pertains to particular data types is spread across several different files but uses the same namespace. This makes importing difficult. As best I can tell, it is an attempt to use a single feature to simultaneously cater to the following concerns:

  1. "We want a proper taxonomy, where e.g. the definitions of how a group works go in Mathlib.Algebra.Group and the theorems about what that means go in Mathlib.GroupTheory."
  2. "We want dot notation to make sense."
  3. "We want building a file (and its import chain) to take at most a moderate amount of time."

Coming from more conventional programming languages, one thing that I'd like is to be able to import something like Subgroup and have access to all of the "methods" (dot-notation-enabled functions) that are defined on that type. I, personally, don't care which file defines those methods; I care about what I can do with a Subgroup. Mathlib does not cater to this. You have to know which file you want. Or, more commonly, you have to know which three files you want.

On the topic of the blog post, I stumbled across it in March: #new members > generalized field notation vs namespaces

It's worth noting, as I was complaining about there, that DNRO doesn't work with the Function namespace. You have to define your methods in _root_.Function. But not to worry; as I learned in that thread, that's how things are supposed to work:

Why do you consider adding definitions to an existing "global" namespace polluting that namespace?

Julia Markus Himmel said:

it went under everyone's radar, but the feature is actually a big deal

No, I very well remember this feature and thought it was a really bad regression. IMO it makes the naming convention story much harder to explain...
The point of namespacing was to avoid cross polluting APIs, but now you can have Foo.Bar contaminating Baz.Bar.

I'm not sure I follow. At least in the following example, this doesn't seem to happen:

namespace Baz

structure Bar where

end Baz

namespace Foo.Bar

def a (_ : Baz.Bar) : Nat := 0

end Foo.Bar

open Foo Bar Baz

variable (x : Baz.Bar)

#check x.a -- Invalid field `a`

Can you show an example of the behavior you're unhappy with?
I think this was also discussed in this thread: #lean4 > dot notation and open

and also in these:
#mathlib4 > TopLevelA.TopLevelB
#new members > generalized field notation vs namespaces
#mathlib4 > Namespace confusion

I tested out the worry I had with (eg) Finset.Nat. in the first of those threads, and it seems less confusing to me now than it did then - I'm not sure if something changed, but the behaviour I'm observing now feels reasonable.

btw this feature still fails for Function:

def Foo.List.IsCool (l : List Nat) : Prop := l = []
/-- info: List.IsCool [1] : Prop -/
#guard_msgs in
open Foo in
#check [1].IsCool

def Foo.Function.IsCool (f : Nat → Nat) : Prop := f = id
/-- error: Unknown constant `id.IsCool` -/
#guard_msgs in
open Foo in
#check id.IsCool

lean4#13244 fixes it but it's stuck on "needs some community discussion", so maybe this hype thread for the feature is the place

My main problem with this feature is that it doesn't work to just be in the namespace. You have to additionally open the namespace:

namespace Foo

def List.bar (l : List α) : List α := l

variable (l : List α)

/--
error: Invalid field `bar`: The environment does not contain `List.bar`, so it is not possible to project the field `bar` from an expression
  l
of type `List α`
-/
#guard_msgs in
#check l.bar

open Foo

/-- info: List.bar l : List α -/
#guard_msgs in
#check l.bar

Julia Markus Himmel said:

I'm not sure I follow. At least in the following example, this doesn't seem to happen:

Okay, sorry, I was unclear above. My unease with this feature isn't the use that you've made of it, namely to allow dot notation on a private function, but rather that it would allow things like namespacing all of mathlib, even though we really want to communicate to our users that eg the mathlib functions in the List namespace are a public extension of the API in core/batteries. When I said pollution above, I rather meant that people writing Baz might not consider relying on Foo.Bar since it's outside their dependency Foo's namespace, and might instead write their own Baz.Bar (with a priori no guarantee that it's identical/compatible with Foo.Bar) and suddenly we have code duplication ("pollution", but not in the sense you understood it).

Yaël Dillies said:

it would allow things like namespacing all of mathlib

This in particular is the reason that I was glad to see the feature quickly forgotten in the community
Yes, I agree that as most Lean features, it can be used both productively and unproductively.

Yaël Dillies said:

Julia Markus Himmel said:

I'm not sure I follow. At least in the following example, this doesn't seem to happen:

Okay, sorry, I was unclear above. My unease with this feature isn't the use that you've made of it, namely to allow dot notation on a private function, but rather that it would allow things like namespacing all of mathlib,...When I said pollution above, I rather meant that people writing Baz might not consider relying on Foo.Bar since it's outside their dependency Foo's namespace, and might instead write their own Baz.Bar

I don't understand why this is a concern. As a programmer and user, I explicitly want to be able to pick and choose which parts of mathlib I use and which ones I replace with my own definitions (and this is true for any language in general).
As an end-user, being able to namespace away mathlib, and then cherry-pick the bits I like is a huge bonus.
